title: Security review: data ephemerality & KMS onboarding — NorthGate Systems

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-11-03
Time: 15:00 PST / 23:00 UTC
Duration: 57 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood), Jordan Patel (Redwood), Alejandra Ruiz (Redwood CSM), Elena Morales (NorthGate CISO), Ravi Kapoor (NorthGate Head of Platform), Sofia Li (NorthGate Legal), Marcus Reed (NorthGate DevOps)

Summary (auto): High level security/compliance review touching on SOC 2, SSO/RBAC, audit logging, KMS and data residency. Customer requested explicit no-training commitment and architecture for customer-managed keys and EU residency.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I think we have a pretty full agenda but we'll focus on the security items you flagged. Elena, thanks for coordinating.
[00:12] Elena Morales: Sure thanks. Wanted to make sure we cover both technical and legal points — like audit logs, who's got access to them, and the no-train commit we're asking about.
[00:22] Jordan Patel: Great, we'll run through our SOC 2 posture, RBAC and SSO, and then dig into KMS and the retention stuff. I have a diagram I'm going to reference — I'll drop a link after the call.
[00:35] Ravi Kapoor: Quick note, we're particularly sensitive to PHI flows in a couple services, plus we need EU residency for a subset of datasets; Frankfurt region preferred.
[00:45] Jordan Patel: Understood. On the EU region, we can pin model serving and logs to the Frankfurt cluster. There's a private deployment option that keeps the control plane in our environment or a customer-managed VPC.
[00:58] Marcus Reed: When you say private deployment, do you mean VPC peering or an on-prem package? Need clarity.
[01:05] Alejandra Ruiz: We have both flavors. For strict residency & KMS control customers typically choose private (VPC) deployment with customer-managed KMS — avoids data leaving region.
[01:20] Elena Morales: And about training — we need a clear, auditable statement that Redwood does not use our prompts or responses to train models. That has to be contractual.
[01:30] Maya Chen: That's a common ask. We provide a no-training option; operationally we have an account flag that opts datasets out of any internal training pipelines. We'll share language for the contract.
[01:41] Sofia Li: When you say "opt out", is there any risk that aggregated telemetry could be used? We need specifics.
[01:48] Jordan Patel: Good question. Telemetry for platform health (errors, latencies) is aggregated and does not contain PII/PHI. For customers who require stricter controls we can suppress telemetry or route it through their VPC to be processed by them.
[02:03] Elena Morales: Can you point me to audit logs — what fields are in the log, retention defaults, and how we can get them?
[02:12] Jordan Patel: Logs include request ID, timestamp, model variant, route, token counts, error codes, and a hashed placeholder for prompt id — but not the full prompt by default in hosted. In private deployments you can configure full request logging or ephemeral-only. Retention defaults to 30 days in hosted, but configurable in Dedicated/Private.
[02:32] Marcus Reed: That bit about hashed placeholder — we will need the raw prompt in the PoC for debugging, but flushed after 7 days. Is that doable?
[02:40] Jordan Patel: Yes, PoC config can enable full request capture for a specific timeframe, then we can auto-delete per retention policy. We'll show the admin UI controls.
[02:50] Ravi Kapoor: KMS — we require FIPS-validated HSM for key material. Does Redwood support customer-managed KMS with an HSM that meets FIPS 140-2/3?
[03:00] Jordan Patel: We integrate with major cloud KMS providers and we support customer-managed keys via bring-your-own-key. For on-prem we can integrate with HSMs — we'll provide the compatibility matrix. Note: our hosted control plane can also be configured to never have plaintext keys — envelope encryption pattern.
[03:18] Elena Morales: Can you give an example flow — who rotates keys and who has access? We need RBAC mapped to roles for audit.
[03:26] Jordan Patel: Sure. Typically customer creates and rotates keys in their KMS. The service uses an encrypted data key that's wrapped by the customer key. Admin RBAC roles control who in your org can request key rotation events, and we log key usage events in audit logs. We'll provide an example event stream.
[03:42] Sofia Li: For legal: we need the logs to show who accessed what and when, and immutable audit trail for at least 2 years. Is that supported?
[03:51] Jordan Patel: Immutable retention depends on deployment. For private deployments on your infrastructure you can ship logs to your SIEM and retain for 2 years. For hosted we have retention tiers and append-only audit logs with export capabilities; we'll get you the SLA for retention and export APIs.
[04:07] Elena Morales: SOC 2 — do you have current Type II? And do you share the bridge letter for scoped controls?
[04:14] Maya Chen: Yes, current SOC 2 Type II is available — we'll attach the report. We also have ISO alignment documentation showing controls mapped to common frameworks.
[04:22] Elena Morales: Great. Please mark the SOC 2 evidence for the security team to review.
[04:28] Maya Chen: Will do.
[04:32] [00:04:32 - 00:10:00 — mid-call technical dive, Jordan shares screen — link: https://redwood.example.com/security/kms-whitepaper]
[04:33] Jordan Patel: I'm sharing the KMS diagram now. The critical part is the envelope encryption flow and how the data plane never has persistent plaintext without customer keys. Note that for Dedicated we can restrict key usage to instances in the region.
[04:47] Elena Morales: If we use customer-managed keys in Frankfurt, can you guarantee that key wrapping/unwrapping operations do not cross regions?
[04:56] Jordan Patel: Yes, we can route crypto ops to region-local endpoints; we'll show the routing policy config. There are tradeoffs for latency but it's straightforward.
[05:07] Marcus Reed: About prompt retention: what are the retention options? We're comfortable with ephemeral prompts (no storage), but need to keep a small debug window up to 7 days.
[05:17] Jordan Patel: Hosted defaults are 30 days for debugging telemetry, but you can set ephemeral-only or custom retention per route. Private deployments give you full control.
[05:27] Ravi Kapoor: And PII/PHI redaction — do you do automatic redaction?
[05:33] Jordan Patel: We offer optional pre-processing filters that can mask or redact known PII/PHI patterns before they hit the model. That can be configured in the request pipeline or via a pre-proxy in your VPC.
[05:45] Elena Morales: Excellent. On the contractual no-training clause — can Redwood commit to not using our data for model improvement under any circumstances unless we opt in?
[05:55] Maya Chen: Yes, we can provide a contractual affirmation. Operationally, that means your account is flagged and data is excluded from any internal training buckets. We will share the exact operational controls and audit evidence.
[06:06] Sofia Li: We'll want an attestation and a mechanism to audit that exclusion — logs showing which accounts had the flag and when.
[06:14] Jordan Patel: We can provide admin audit events for the opt-out flag, and show exports for the exclusion list over time.
[06:22] Elena Morales: For incident response: access to logs and a runbook — if there's a breach who do we talk to and what's the SLA?
[06:29] Maya Chen: Our incident response includes a 24x7 pager for critical incidents for enterprise customers, and designated point-of-contact. We'll share the IR runbook and the escalation matrix.
[06:40] Ravi Kapoor: Are penetration test results available?
[06:43] Maya Chen: Yes, we have summaries and remediation status. We'll share the redacted pentest report.
[06:49] Marcus Reed: About RBAC and SSO: we use Okta and provisioning via SCIM. Can you support SCIM group sync and role mapping to fine-grained permissions?
[06:58] Jordan Patel: Absolutely. We support SAML SSO and SCIM for provisioning. You can map SCIM groups to product roles (admin, ops, read-only) and apply per-route permissions.
[07:09] Elena Morales: One more: legal requires that the data processing addendum includes data residency guarantees and a clear definition of processing vs storage.
[07:17] Sofia Li: And definitions for de-identification and pseudonymization — we need language that meets GDPR expectations.
[07:24] Maya Chen: We'll coordinate with our legal ops and provide a DPA template showing residency commitments and pseudonymization language.
[07:33] [crosstalk]
[07:36] Alejandra Ruiz: For the PoC, Jordan and I will own setup and metrics (latency, token costs, log flow). We'll propose a 2-week window in Frankfurt and configure KMS with a customer key if desired.
[07:49] Elena Morales: That works. Can we also test the admin audit exports so our security team can ingest them into Splunk?
[07:56] Jordan Patel: Yes, we'll export syslog/JSON stream and provide a sample ingestion config.
[08:04] Sofia Li: For no-training clause, I'll send the baseline wording we prefer. That will speed up legal review.
[08:11] Maya Chen: Perfect. We'll assemble artifacts and send them by next week.
[08:16] [00:08:16 — wrap up recap]
[08:17] Maya Chen: Quick recap: we will send SOC2 and pentest summary, KMS/HSM whitepaper, PoC runbook for Frankfurt private deployment, sample admin audit export, and initial contract language for no-train. Any other items?
[08:28] Elena Morales: Please also include the retention configuration UI screenshots and the API for programmatic deletion.
[08:33] Jordan Patel: Noted — retention UI + deletion APIs will be included.
[08:38] Marcus Reed: Also include an example of the hashed placeholder behavior and how to enable full capture for the PoC.
[08:44] Jordan Patel: Will include examples.
[08:47] Sofia Li: Thanks everyone.
[08:50] Maya Chen: Thanks all — we'll follow up with the artifacts and a calendar invite for the PoC kickoff.
[08:56] [meeting ends]

Notes:
- Shared artifacts: SOC 2 Type II (link to secure portal), KMS whitepaper (link), retention UI screenshots (attached), PoC runbook (to be shared).
- Slight transcription errors likely where technical acronyms were said quickly (e.g., FIPS, SCIM, KV cache pronounced as "kay-vee").

End of transcript.
